Girolamo Savonarola
ji-ROL-uh-mo sa-vo-nuh-ROH-luh
proper noun (figure)
Italian Girolamo — the Italian form of Jerome (Greek Hieronymos, "sacred name"). Surname Savonarola from the Ferrarese-Florentine family of his father, of uncertain medieval derivation.

📖 Biblical Definition

Girolamo Savonarola (September 21, 1452 — May 23, 1498 AD) was a Dominican friar and prophet-preacher of Renaissance Florence whose four-year reign of moral-religious reform (1494-1498) over the most cosmopolitan and humanist city in Europe ended in his excommunication, torture, and burning at the stake in the Piazza della Signoria — the same square where, three years earlier, he had organized the "Bonfire of the Vanities" in which Florentines voluntarily burned their luxury goods, pagan books, and erotic art. Born in Ferrara to a physician's family; entered the Dominican order at twenty-three; assigned to the priory of San Marco in Florence (1490); rose to prominence preaching dramatically apocalyptic sermons predicting the imminent scourging of the Italian church and the conversion of the Turks. When the French king Charles VIII invaded Italy in 1494 and the Medici were expelled from Florence, Savonarola's prophecies seemed vindicated and he became the de facto theocratic ruler of the city. For four years he reformed Florentine morals, abolished gambling and prostitution, and preached unflinching denunciation of Pope Alexander VI Borgia's corruption. The Borgia pope excommunicated him in 1497; the Florentines turned against him in 1498; he was tortured and burned. His program contained the seeds of the Reformation a generation later (Luther read him in 1521 and wrote favorably of him), but his apocalyptic prophecies, his theocratic experiment, and his confidence that he had received personal divine revelation cannot be assimilated to the Reformation without serious qualification. He prepared the ground; he was not the harvest.

Italian Dominican friar and prophet-preacher (1452-1498 AD); de facto theocratic ruler of Florence 1494-1498; led the Bonfire of the Vanities; excommunicated by Alexander VI Borgia; tortured and burned 1498.

GIROLAMO SAVONAROLA, proper noun. Italian Girolamo (Italian form of Jerome, Greek Hieronymos, "sacred name") + Savonarola, family name.

Dominican friar and prophet-preacher of Florence (1452-1498 AD); de facto theocratic ruler of Florence after the Medici expulsion (1494-1498); led the Bonfire of the Vanities (February 1497).

Excommunicated by Pope Alexander VI Borgia; tortured and burned in the Piazza della Signoria on May 23, 1498. Read appreciatively by Luther; not fully assimilable to the Reformation.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Savonarola is corrupted when his Bonfire of the Vanities is romanticized as picturesque Renaissance theater rather than read with serious thought about coercive moral reform, when his apocalyptic-prophetic claims are uncritically endorsed by anti-Catholic Protestants, or when his courageous denunciation of Borgia corruption is severed from his serious theological errors.

expand to see more

Apocalyptic-prophet-uncritical-endorsement. Savonarola repeatedly claimed direct revelation from God in his sermons, predicted specific historical events (the French invasion, the death of Lorenzo de' Medici, the imminent scourging of the church), and built his Florentine theocracy on the premise that his prophetic word stood alongside Scripture. The Reformation tradition rejected exactly this kind of post-canonical prophetic claim. Honor his courage against Borgia corruption; do not assimilate his prophetic-revelation framework. The closed canon is the rule.

Theocratic-coercion sentimentalization. The Bonfire of the Vanities (February 7, 1497) is sometimes painted as a charming Florentine spiritual exercise. It was actually a state-organized public destruction of property — books, art, musical instruments, mirrors, cosmetics, women's gowns — gathered by youth gangs from house to house and burned in the city square. The reform was coerced, not voluntary in any meaningful sense for the people whose property burned. The Reformed reader honors Savonarola's witness against ecclesiastical corruption without endorsing the coercive Florentine theocracy he built; the gospel calls for repentance from the heart, not legislation from the magistracy.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Italian Girolamo ("sacred name," from Greek Hieronymos, the Italian form of Jerome) + Florentine family surname. The friar-prophet of Florence (d. 1498); read appreciatively by Luther a generation later.

expand to see more

Italian Girolamo — Italian form of Jerome (Greek Hieronymos, "sacred name")

Family name Savonarola of Ferrarese-Florentine derivation

Dominican friar at San Marco, Florence; de facto theocratic ruler of the city 1494-1498

Led the Bonfire of the Vanities, February 7, 1497; excommunicated 1497; tortured and burned May 23, 1498

Read appreciatively by Luther in the 1520s; Luther's edition of Savonarola's Meditations on Psalms 31 and 51 appeared with Luther's preface in 1523

Usage

"Savonarola — the Dominican preacher whose four-year Florentine theocracy ended in the same square where his Bonfire had burned three years earlier."

"Pre-Reformation prophet of corruption-denunciation; not a Reformer in the doctrinal sense, but read warmly by Luther."

"A complex figure: courageous against the Borgia pope, mistaken in his apocalyptic prophecies, sincere in his Christ-centered devotion."
